recent_candidates.title: Top Democrat vows to increase oversight of intelligence agencies
recent_candidates.author: Brendan Ruberry
recent_candidates.excerpt: The top Democrat in charge of overseeing US intelligence agencies in the next Congress vowed Wednesday to increase oversight of the Trump administration’s expanded use of covert action. The White House has reportedly increased spy agencies’ footprint in Mexico and Latin America, and against adversaries in cyberspace , while also firing hundreds of longtime officials. Rep. Jim Himes said the investigations would probe whether officials “were fired because they said something that was inconsistent with what the president wanted to be true .” Congress is also looking to scrutinize a rash of 11 or more suicides this year at US cyber agencies, where workload has surged in the past year in response to escalating foreign conflicts, Bloomberg reported. — Brendan Ruberry

recent_candidates.title: Nvidia CEO scandal exposes gaps in US chip controls
recent_candidates.author: Brendan Ruberry
recent_candidates.excerpt: A Chinese university with ties to the country’s military was able to obtain Nvidia’s most powerful chips last month despite being on a US blacklist, Reuters reported, as scrutiny over the chipmaker reveals holes in Washington’s regulatory framework. The disclosure comes as lawmakers press the Trump administration on its investigation into Megaspeed, the Singapore firm at the center of the Jensen Huang spy scandal, amid reports that the Commerce Department has delayed efforts to blacklist the company suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China. US restrictions have accelerated Beijing’s efforts to develop homegrown semiconductors — independence that will allow it “to scale faster than the US,” Semafor’s tech editor argued: Nvidia, crucial to the US’ advantage, will be “ fundamentally weakened ” without Huang. — Brendan Ruberry

recent_candidates.title: CoreWeave results drive broad tech rally
recent_candidates.author: Brendan Ruberry
recent_candidates.excerpt: US tech stocks surged Wednesday following stronger-than-expected CoreWeave earnings, as the AI trade recovered after last week’s selloff. Despite the company’s massive borrowing, investors were encouraged by CoreWeave beating revenue expectations and raising its forecast, as traders parsed the key Anthropic vendor’s results for clues ahead of the AI firm’s planned IPO next week. CoreWeave shares, though, are down 20% so far this year , and the company is not throwing enough cash off its business to cover its roughly $41 billion of net debt, amid jitters over the sustainability of the AI buildout. Still, “a healthier-looking CoreWeave today at least provides some reassurance to the broader AI market and especially to Anthropic,” a Bloomberg columnist wrote. — Brendan Ruberry

recent_candidates.title: Klobuchar successor talk centers on second-term House member
recent_candidates.author: Burgess Everett
recent_candidates.excerpt: Democrats are starting to debate who will succeed Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., when she’s sworn in as governor next year. There’s one name that keeps coming up: Democratic Rep. Kelly Morrison, who just won her second term to the House and served in the state legislature before that. Klobuchar hasn’t made a final decision on the pick, according to a person familiar with her thinking. But many Democrats believe Morrison is a frontrunner after she passed on the 2026 Senate race. Asked if she wants the appointment, Morrison said only that she’s “excited” about Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan and about representing her district: “The governor-elect will appoint someone, and I know she’ll be right by the people of Minnesota.” Rep. Angie Craig, D-Minn., who lost the Senate primary to Flanagan, is seen as a longshot for the appointment.

recent_candidates.title: Omar wants to get back on House Foreign Affairs Committee
recent_candidates.author: Nicholas Wu
recent_candidates.excerpt: Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., wants to get back on the House Foreign Affairs Committee after Republicans removed her, though she’s also angling for a spot on the Appropriations panel. “I would love to,” she told Semafor of Foreign Affairs. “That is my favorite committee. ... I’m thinking of Approps and other committees, so we’ll see how it all shakes out.” If she were to return to the Foreign Affairs Committee, she could lead its Africa subpanel because of her seniority. The subcommittee’s current top Democrat, Rep. Sara Jacobs, D-Calif., said “it’s still being figured out.” But Rep. Greg Meeks, D-N.Y., the committee’s top Democrat, said it’s Omar’s “choice” whether to chair the Africa subpanel. House Democrats will soon start the process of populating committees, and with a larger-than-expected House majority, they’ll face some tough decisions about divvying up spots, especially on sought-after panels.

recent_candidates.title: West Wing reshuffles as Miller settles in
recent_candidates.author: Shelby Talcott
recent_candidates.excerpt: More changes are expected across the White House in the coming weeks as Stephen Miller settles into his new role as chief of staff, with some aides who worked closely with Susie Wiles shifting into new roles. A White House official told Semafor that Meghan Bauer, who heads the Office of Cabinet Affairs, will shift to a different role in the White House. (Multiple other sources, however, suggested to Semafor that Bauer is expected to depart in the coming weeks.) Meanwhile, Walker Barrett, a senior policy adviser to Wiles, will move under the deputy chief of staff for policy, the official said. The staffing changes offer an early glimpse of how the West Wing is reshuffling as Trump and Miller reshape the team post-midterms. It remains unclear how many more aides will change assignments or depart ahead of the new year.

recent_candidates.title: Local media startup City Cast reshuffles leadership
recent_candidates.author: Max Tani
recent_candidates.excerpt: The locally-focused media startup City Cast has named Andi McDaniel, the company’s chief creative officer, its new CEO, replacing David Plotz. City Cast launched in 2021 as a local podcast and newsletter venture aimed at serving cities where local news was shifting from old newspapers and radio to screens. The company has since expanded to 13 cities, including Austin, Las Vegas, and Philadelphia, among others. “This next chapter for us is about expanding audiences. It’s about adapting to AI, and it’s about making the business successful,” McDaniel, a veteran public radio executive and co-founder of City Cast , told Semafor. City Cast has gained greater visibility in recent months, primarily for its expansion in its hometown. As Semafor first noted last year, in response to what the company saw as an opportunity created by the turbulence at The Washington Post, City Cast scaled up its newsroom and business in Washington. City Cast is backed by Graham Holdings, which owned the Post before selling to Jeff Bezos. City Cast DC now has 20 people on staff, and said it has found some success attracting a younger audience to its content, tripling the size of people it reaches regularly from roughly 100,000 at the beginning of the year to around 300,000. Not every bet has paid off. The company shuttered two arms, in Boise and Houston. recent_candidates.title: Airwallex’s CEO isn't worried about AI
recent_candidates.author: Reed Albergotti
recent_candidates.excerpt: Jack Zhang isn’t worried about AI taking over global finance, but he is concerned about cybersecurity. Zhang co-founded Australian fintech unicorn Airwallex, which allows businesses to make cross-border payments and manage finances in dozens of countries, and is now morphing into an agentic finance company. Zhang joined Future Proof to discuss how his company is using AI to build systems to help companies handle their finances — essentially building an AI-managed CFO office. The company currently relies mainly on ChatGPT and Claude, but Zhang also said it’s looking at developing proprietary models using open-weight solutions. Zhang doesn’t think AI will get so good that it can entirely replace humans, at least not in his field. “The laws still require you to have somebody sign off as auditor, and how the auditor does that sign-off can be assisted by agents,” he said. “I don’t think we can completely get rid of the human in the loop.” What Zhang is “very, very, very, very worried” about is cybersecurity. With news about cyber breaches emerging almost daily, the company is tackling the issue by using behavioral monitoring and hiring experts from the Australian Department of Defence and Palantir, among other strategies. “We’re moving hundreds of billions of dollars today ... We’re constantly paranoid about how good our defense [is] against this type of threat,” he said. — Reed Albergotti

recent_candidates.title: Nvidia is more than a chip company
recent_candidates.author: Reed Albergotti
recent_candidates.excerpt: Reed’s view Nvidia has been battered over the past couple of days, but it could get worse. That is, if founder and CEO Jensen Huang is forced or chooses to step down, or if investigations pin him down for doing something illegal. In most sectors of the economy, CEOs are expected to run businesses well, but they are generally interchangeable parts — albeit expensive ones. Google and Apple show that founder CEOs, which are harder to replicate, can be replaced. But even among founder CEOs, Huang stands apart for bold bets that helped him endure short-term suffering in return for long-term gain. Most people know Nvidia for the climbing stock in their portfolios, or the GPUs on every tech company’s Christmas list. But his creation of the CUDA platform in 2006 is perhaps the best example of how he’s been able to step ahead of the industry for decades. Nvidia’s computing platform and programming model, the software that essentially underpins the modern AI industry, created one of the most valuable moats in business history. A half dozen years later, seeing the progress in neural networks, he pivoted to AI. Huang realized AI would require massive data centers with interconnected chips, and concluded that networking would become the bottleneck. He bet billions on the development of NVLink, a nervous system that allows discrete GPUs to act as one massive supercomputer, and the $6.9 billion acquisition of Mellanox Technologies, the Israeli networking company, in 2019. recent_candidates.title: Progressives try to have it both ways on Medicare for All
recent_candidates.author: Nicholas Wu
recent_candidates.excerpt: The News Progressive Democrats are trying a tricky feat as their party takes power : endorsing Medicare for All while quietly pushing for smaller steps toward it. Their dilemma began with the party’s remarkable midterm success. Democrats are united in attributing their electoral triumph in part to voter backlash against GOP healthcare moves — and this year, even purple-district candidates won while backing Medicare for All. But now, the left is split on how to make it happen. Without a filibuster or veto-proof majority in Congress next year, Democrats are calibrating their expectations for change based on what can potentially pass through the maneuver known as reconciliation, which requires only a simple majority. Some progressives are calling for a unified drive to lower the Medicare eligibility age, add guaranteed coverage up to age 19, and add dental and vision coverage. That could offer a middle ground for party leaders who are looking to stave off fights over bills likely to be vetoed by President Donald Trump. Embracing a big step toward pure Medicare for All could also hand a victory to progressives who have long pushed for legislative action — if they can settle for something less than the litmus test they set up. “It’s the perfect way for us to get ready for the next trifecta if we pass those three bills, and then if we mark up the entire Medicare for All bill,” said Rep. recent_candidates.title: Mississippi elects Democrat Scott Colom to Senate in massive upset
recent_candidates.author: By Jason Beeferman
recent_candidates.excerpt: Mississippi voted blue, in a shock win for Democrats. Democrat Scott Colom ousted Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in a state that went for President Donald Trump by 23 points in 2024. He will be the first Black senator elected in Mississippi since the Reconstruction era — and the first Democrat from the state headed to the Senate in 44 years. Colom, a Democratic district attorney, ran a scrappy campaign that saw some national money and resources in the final stretch of the race. Hyde-Smith was appointed to the Senate in 2018 and had since won election to the seat twice, but she faced attacks from Colom that she was out of touch and indifferent to rising grocery and gas prices during Trump’s second term. National Democratic groups hadn't paid much attention to the Mississippi Senate race until an October surge of excitement for Colom drew late spending and attention. Colom's win is a boost to the Democratic Party as it seeks to gain a larger foothold in the South and improve their standing with Black voters. It’s also a major vindication for Colom and other Southern Democrats who argued Mississippi had been neglected for far too long.

recent_candidates.title: Biden says he wouldn't have run in 2024 if he knew about his cancer
recent_candidates.author: By Gregory Svirnovskiy
recent_candidates.excerpt: Former President Joe Biden would not have run for reelection in 2024 if he had known about his cancer, he said in an interview released Wednesday in which he also sought to downplay the historic debate performance that helped end his political career. "If I had known that I was feeling lousy because I had cancer, I would have not gone forward because I don't think an 80-year-old man with cancer should be running," he said in the interview with People magazine , which was conducted last week following Democrats’ big midterm wins and ahead of his upcoming memoir’s release. The former president announced his diagnosis — Stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer — in May 2025, just four months after leaving the White House. It triggered an outpouring of public support — but it also raised questions about how doctors failed to catch the cancer earlier and whether it might have contributed to Biden’s apparent decline toward the end of his term. “I think it’s very sad, actually. I’m surprised that it wasn’t, you know, the public wasn’t notified a long time ago because to get to [a Gleason score of] 9, that’s a long time,” President Donald Trump told reporters shortly after Biden’s announcement. Prior to his diagnosis, Biden hadn’t been screened for prostate cancer since 2014 . U.S. guidelines have long recommended that men shouldn't be screened for the cancer once they hit their 70s. recent_candidates.title: Several Dem women leaned into their identity this cycle. Not in the way you think.
recent_candidates.author: By Lauren Fedor and Erin Doherty
recent_candidates.excerpt: When Annie Andrews announced her longshot campaign for U.S. Senate last May, the Democrat from South Carolina pitched herself as a “busy mom.” “Lindsey [Graham] is going to tell you I am radical, that I am crazy,” Andrews said in her launch video . “But here’s the thing: I am literally a busy mom and a pediatrician who plays peek-a-boo with my patients, watches Bluey with my kids … and spends most of my free time shuttling them to dance, Tae Kwon Do and football.” Now, she is one of a record number of women who will serve in the next Congress. And as a 46-year-old mother of three school-aged children, she’s among several Democratic women who flipped seats and governor’s mansions this November with campaign messages centered on parenting and affordability. It’s a notable campaign shift from previous election cycles: This year, female candidates focused less on the historic nature of their bids, or culture war issues that have long fomented divisions over gender and electability. Instead, they zeroed in on an economic message emphasizing bread-and-butter concerns — like how rising costs were squeezing families, including theirs. “Moms understand kitchen table issues better than perhaps anyone,” said Jessica Mackler, president of EMILY’s List, the group that recruits and backs female Democratic candidates who support abortion rights. “They understand how to stretch a paycheck. recent_candidates.title: To Preserve Collegiate Competition, Constrain It
recent_candidates.author: Asheesh Agarwal
recent_candidates.excerpt: To paraphrase an infamous paradox, can the government create a competitive regime so dysfunctional that even the government can’t save it? Due to a mishmash of litigation and legislation, as well as $21 billion in revenue , today’s college sports landscape resembles neither an academic paradise nor a capitalist utopia, but rather Thomas Hobbes’s war of all against all. Every “student-athlete” becomes a free agent every year. Schools change conferences heedless of geographic or historical ties. One state allows pro athletes to play college ball while many schools lose tens of millions annually on their athletic departments. Football and men’s basketball, the revenue sports, effectively subsidize the Olympic and women’s sports, yet Name, Image, and Likeness (NIL) dollars may soon bring this model to an end. Against this backdrop, the best way to preserve competition in college athletics may be, in fact, to limit it. As Neal McCluskey suggests in his forum lead , a limited antitrust exemption would allow the NCAA to create a sustainable competitive landscape in which numerous schools could continue to compete in the revenue sports, schools would have incentives to support nonrevenue sports, and student-athletes could profit off their athletic ability. recent_candidates.author: Rebecca Burgess
recent_candidates.excerpt: Editor’s note: This essay was originally published on May 25, 2026. Crisp against the gloaming, a bugle sounds a rising then falling strain. It’s 5 pm. It’s cold. Yet in the nation’s capital, something embers. While DC’s iPhone-occupied evening toilers and travelers scurry about to their next diversion, the lone uniformed Doughboy standing at 1400 Pennsylvania Avenue signals a time-honored but incongruous musical thought of reflection for day’s ending. My feet or my heart or my head have drawn me back here again, to the inscribed words, the murmuring water splatting, and the parading in bronze—of the human, and of the nation—that all together make up America’s newest national monument, the National World War I Memorial, at Pershing Park . Alongside its American precursor, the French version of “Taps,” la sonnerie “Aux Morts,” was sounded. Dignified French and American speakers at the event reminded their audience that between their respective militaries is the “oldest continuous military friendship our [American] nation has ever known.” Such words are fitly sounded here, mere steps south from Lafayette Square and the White House, and within the statuesque hearing of the general tasked with America’s arguably first physical repayment of its Revolutionary War debt to France, with Pershing’s command of the American Expeditionary Forces (AEF) onto French soil. recent_candidates.title: Tech CEOs circle wagons around Huang despite China spy claims
recent_candidates.author: Margaux Maccoll
recent_candidates.excerpt: Billionaire Nvidia founder Jensen Huang, who is currently holding the entire U.S. economy on his leather jacket-wearing back, has allegedly been canoodling with an AI executive-turned-Chinese spy. You might expect this news to terrify Silicon Valley, the home of the new age defense contractors. You might expect calls for Huang's head. Not exactly. “He did something incredibly dumb,” Shaun Maguire, an investor at Silicon Valley giant Sequoia Capital, posted on X . However, “I believe Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership.” Jason Calacanis of the All-In Podcast joined in. “Jensen and NVIDIA’s technology are a critical target, and we need to protect them both," he wrote . The tepid reaction shows a splintering of the tech-China hawk movement. Moguls in this space have spent the last few years spreading fear over China’s potential AI dominance — in part because of a belief in American exceptionalism, but also out of fierce self-interest. But what happens now that one of their own has potentially threatened said AI dominance? “Saving Jensen is right now the cause in the VC world,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution. Up until last month, Huang was the platonic ideal of a tech founder. A regular on the podcast circuit, Huang was a chatty AI optimist with a squicky-clean reputation and a wife of over forty years he met at engineering school. recent_candidates.title: Iran War Day 257: Iran Threatens U.S. Bases in Europe
recent_candidates.author: Luke Nicastro
recent_candidates.excerpt: Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said Wednesday Iran would strike U.S. bases in Europe if they were used to launch attacks. “If American aircraft take off from an American military base, even one located in a European country or some other distant region, to bomb Iran, we will strike those bases as well,” Rezaei told a Lebanese outlet in an interview. The statement is the most explicit threat yet issued against U.S. installations outside the Middle East. Separately, an Iranian news agency also quoted Rezaei as saying that Iran “will not remove even a single particle of enriched nuclear material from the country.” Also on Wednesday, the insurer Allianz said in a report the Iran War would likely cost Gulf countries more than $200 billion in damage to physical infrastructure. Factoring in other economic effects, like tourism and trade impacts, the report put the total cost of the war at around $790 billion through 2030. Oil prices have remained below recent highs: Brent crude opened around $92 per barrel, and AAA reports that the average price of regular gasoline in the United States is $3.94 per gallon. The post Iran War Day 257: Iran Threatens U.S. Bases in Europe appeared first on The American Conservative .

recent_candidates.title: Jim Jordan Elected New House GOP Leader
recent_candidates.author: Luke Nicastro
recent_candidates.excerpt: House Republicans chose Rep. Jim Jordan (R-OH) to be their next leader in a closed-door meeting Tuesday. Jordan, a founder of the Freedom Caucus and close ally of President Donald Trump, beat out Rep. Steve Scalise (R-LA) in a 106-73 vote. As House Majority Leader, Scalise had worked closely with outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA); Jordan’s victory is widely seen as signalling a break with Johnson’s leadership. Following Republicans’ disastrous showing in last week’s midterm elections, Jordan will lead his party as it enters the minority come January. The post Jim Jordan Elected New House GOP Leader appeared first on The American Conservative .

recent_candidates.title: Hegseth Survives Impeachment Effort
recent_candidates.author: Jude Russo
recent_candidates.excerpt: The House voted Tuesday to send the impeachment articles against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to committee for further consideration, effectively ending the latest effort from Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY) to oust him. The motion to refer Massie’s articles, which focused on Hegseth’s role in using military force in Iran and the Caribbean without congressional approval, passed 211–204, with 11 Democrats and seven Republicans missing the vote. “Again, Victories in Venezuela and Iran, the Best Recruitment Numbers in the History of the Military (Long waiting lists to get in!), and Spirit like rarely seen before, led to the EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot,” wrote President Donald Trump in a social media post after the vote, in which he also described Massie as a “LOSER.” The post Hegseth Survives Impeachment Effort appeared first on The American Conservative .

recent_candidates.author: James P. Pinkerton
recent_candidates.excerpt: History Precedents for the Vice President: Humphrey or Reagan? The midterms were hard on the GOP, but all is not lost. The vice president is in a difficult spot. His boss, the president, has led the country into an unpopular foreign war. And while nobody thinks the VP ever really supported the decision, as the number two in the White House, he has taken hits. In addition, since the incumbent party has been dominant for so long, popular grievances on a variety of issues have accumulated—and voters have lashed out. No wonder the presidential party suffered a drubbing in the midterms. Since the president himself won’t be running again, the veep is seen as the frontrunner for his party’s nomination in two years. Yet the fear (and for others, the hope) is that POTUS and his unpopular war have poisoned the chalice for any would-be successor. This could be a sketch of Vice President J.D. Vance’s situation—many would say, his predicament . Yet actually, this outlines Vice President Hubert Humphrey’s situation in the 1960s. And we can learn from what happened to him then. recent_candidates.title: Keeping Warfare Irregular This Veterans Day
recent_candidates.author: Kate Espinosa
recent_candidates.excerpt: Every veteran has a story. Irregular warfare (IW) veterans are no different, although their stories are sometimes harder to tell. That’s because IW stories, much like the humans behind them, often operate in the gray area. Sometimes the mission was never publicly acknowledged. Sometimes the greatest measure of success was something that never happened . Today, Americans observe Veterans Day. Across the Atlantic, many of our allies and partners mark Remembrance Day in November, while other countries recognize their veterans and fallen service members on different days throughout the year. The dates may differ, but the underlying sentiment is shared: to recognize the service and sacrifice of those who have served, and to ensure their experiences are not forgotten. That’s where the Irregular Warfare Initiative comes in. We tell the stories that other outlets might shy away from because they don’t fit neatly into a format designed for a commercial audience. recent_candidates.title: SEC enforcement actions drop to multi-decade lows
recent_candidates.author: Brendan Ruberry
recent_candidates.excerpt: Enforcement actions and penalties levied by the US Securities and Exchange Commission have fallen to multi-decade lows, reflecting a dramatic pullback by Wall Street’s top watchdog. The agency, which has seen budget and staff reductions under the Trump administration, doled out $1.1 billion in penalties last year, the lowest in two decades. The decline drew a rebuke from Democrats who vowed increased scrutiny of its enforcement program in the next Congress, though an SEC official cautioned that “ activity and effectiveness are not the same .” While some suggested the figures were consistent with the agency’s stated aim of promoting more IPOs , “the obvious risk is, with less enforcement, you have a greater risk of fraud ,” a law professor told the Financial Times. — Brendan Ruberry

recent_candidates.excerpt: Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia could spell a sea change in China’s AI fortunes, as heightened scrutiny from Washington threatens to choke off the supply of American compute to mainland tech titans and AI startups. On the flipside, restrictions on American compute could benefit Chinese chipmakers with Beijing pushing more resources toward developing semiconductor self-sufficiency. — Brendan Ruberry

recent_candidates.title: SoftBank loses billions after over-ordering AI energy equipment
recent_candidates.author: Chloé Farand
recent_candidates.excerpt: Japanese investor SoftBank reported $3.7 billion hit to its earnings on Tuesday, after cancelling a glut of orders for gas-producing equipment to power the AI hardware buildout that it couldn’t use. The news intensified fears that the AI frenzy that saw hyperscalers take on huge amounts of debt to build the infrastructure needed to power data centres could be losing steam. Nvidia founder Jensen Huang’s resignation has also made investors nervous that the world’s largest chipmaker could back away from its strategy of bankrolling AI hardware under a new leader. “I think the fear is that the music might stop,” a fund manager told Reuters. The AI buildout is still making winners, however. Siemens Energy expects to triple its dividend in 2027 as the US data center boom boosts demand for its gas turbines and grid equipment. “Some of the growth rates for data centers were unrealistic, it’s just that nobody wanted to ​hear it,” said its CEO. recent_candidates.title: Measures restricting clean tech exports slowing down energy transition
recent_candidates.author: Chloé Farand
recent_candidates.excerpt: Major economies representing 58% of the world’s GDP have adopted at least one measure to restrict the import of clean energy technologies, many targeting Chinese goods, according to data published by the Oxford Climate Policy Monitor . In contrast, a large number of small economies outside China, accounting for about 8% of world GDP, are liberalising imports of EVs, batteries, along with wind and solar equipment, creating a de facto free trade area for clean tech. Analysis by the Blavatnik School of Government at the University of Oxford found that restrictions are making the transition slower and more expensive, but they may also be needed to balance effective climate policy with industrial development and economic security . “Openness and protection can be combined, rather than traded off wholesale,” it said. Large economies could pursue more selective trade restrictions instead of trying to build entirely self-sufficient industries, while smaller countries could specialise in particular stages of manufacturing. “Our findings show that many countries have begun to implement this strategy,” said Claas Mertens, the brief’s co-author. — Chloé Farand

recent_candidates.title: Africa to press for more adaptation finance at COP31
recent_candidates.author: Chloé Farand
recent_candidates.excerpt: African countries want the COP31 climate talks, now underway in Türkiye, to set out how the world will deliver on last year’s pledge to triple adaptation finance designed to help cope with the growing impact of extreme weather events. A large share of the money has previously come from aid budgets, which have fallen to their lowest level since 2014 , and most wealthier countries have pledged little-to-no new climate finance from this year . The African Group of Negotiators says addressing this issue is vital to a successful outcome in Antalya as support for the continent’s vulnerabilities has been “dwindling,” according to its chairperson. But even a tripling in financing will not close the gap: In 2024, the amount available for developing economies reached around $30 billion — that pales against the $305 billion the UN estimates they need annually to 2035. Plans have been announced at COP31 to scale up successful adaptation projects and attract larger investments. But these cannot be “entirely dependent on voluntary contributions,” Kenya’s climate envoy told Semafor. — Chloé Farand

recent_candidates.excerpt: It’s two o’clock on a Wednesday afternoon. I’m standing under a seventy-year-old Silver Maple tree to watch a grey squirrel gnaw at a nut. recent_candidates.excerpt: El presidente de Estados Unidos , Donald Trump , ha insistido este jueves en que quiere dejar zanjado «el tema» de Cuba antes de dejar la Casa Blanca dentro de dos años y sigue contemplando la posiblidad de, llegado el caso, lanzar «una breve operación militar» para hacerse con el control de la isla y forzar un cambio de autoridades al estilo venezolano. «Quiero resolver el tema de Cuba antes de irme, y para ello tenemos a un tipo muy bueno y con mucho talento llamado Marco», ha manifestado el presidente en una entrevista a la cadena conservadora Salem News Channel, en referencia a su secretario de Estado Marco Rubio .
